Well I said I would never do it but after watching a bunch of people trying to prove one is better than the other I decided to add my 1/2 cents worth. (1/2 cent is all it's worth)

First of all lets start at the top of the argument.

Just what does every nation want in a military rifle?

  • First it has to be able to do the job. That means that it must put a bullet through a human body with enough force to incapacitate or kill.

  • Second it must be reliable. No nation is going to field a weapon that does not go bang when the trigger is pulled or falls apart on the battlefield.

  • Third is must not cost so much that it will bankrupt a nation so it cannot afford any other weapons.

Where weapons differ is that they kind of mirror a national character. For instance we Americans just love new and innovative stuff. The Russians are a bit more traditional in out look. A perfect example of this is we Americans can now select from about 3000 small craft beers that are brewed to secret recipes in back rooms somewhere. The Russians (Vodka is Vodka and you don't need 3000 manufactures of the stuff.)

Also we must remember that the greatest killer on the battle field is not the rifle but the artillery round. Artillery kill 10 times more people than any rifle. So how do the rifles stack up.

  • First of all lets admit that the M-16 had been dinked with for almost 40 years. (we have played around with twist rates, barrel lengths, different projectiles etc) The Russians on the other hand only made one change in the AK-47 it that same 40 years. (They went from 7.62X39 to a 5.45 X39 cartridge) That seems to suggest that there were some very basic short comings with the original design. We know from experience that the M-16 had problems when first introduced in Viet Nam. We tend to ignore that the Russians had similar problems when the AK-47 when it was introduced in 1948. Work in designing the AK-47 started way back in 1945 when world war II was just wrapping up. The Russians had the lot of experience with being on the wrong end of the Sturmgewher 44. The Sturmgewher 44 fired a 7.92 X33 cartridge that fired a projectile that was 13 grains heavier and about 375 feet per second faster than our .30 carbine.

The driving force behind the Sturmgewher and the AK-47 was the realization that all most all combat engagements occurred at ranges less than 300 meters. Also the Germans realized that volume of fire was more important thing in an engagement. A high volume of fire caused the enemy to keep their heads down while you advanced or retreated. The German doctrine was that killing was to be done with hand grenades or mortar fire. (The Germans were deadly with their Granatwefer 34's ((81.4 mm )) mortars). The Granatwefer 34 fired a 8 lb shell out to 2400 meters.

Back to rifles:
* Both the Germans and Russians had extensive experience in city fighting which also required a high volume of fire at really close quarters. American didn't get involved in city fighting until the end of the war with the invasion of Germany proper.

  • Americans also have had this thing about accuracy. Because of our wide open spaces and limited population we could build 1000 yard rifle ranges any where and because of the 2n Amendment have a ton of rifle matches. Also the (Sport) or Pest eradication of Prairie Dogs and wood chucks aided in the American enchantment with accuracy. So you can see why the Russians went with the AK-47 while we Americans fooled around with the M-14. We wanted a rifle that could kill at a 1000 yards though most infantry men couldn't hit the broad side of a barn beyond 600 meters. The rifle could reach and touch some one at 1000 yards but the shooter couldn't.

The Viet Nam war changed all that. Our Green Berets were fighting in the jungles of Viet Nam While JFK was asking what you could do for your country. Combat in Viet Nam was either Ambush, counter Ambush, or a raid on a location. All these engagements required a high rate of fire from a rifle that was controllable on auto fire and lethal to boot. The M-2 carbine didn't cut it in the lethality department. Into this picture stepped Eugene Stoner and Armalite with a new light weight rifle base on a varmint cartridge from Remington. When the Green Berets tested the rifle in Viet Nam they fell in love with the thing. They could shoot up a storm and carry 300 to 400 rounds with ease. Of course when you took them out of the hands of professionals and gave them to private Snuffy who was more experienced in rolling a joint and getting a girl out of her panties than disassembling and cleaning a weapon troubles abounded. The Army finally sovled the problems but the Rep is still out there.

So where do we go from here. Fist of all let me say that there isn't a dimes worth of difference between the 5.45X39 and the 5.56X45 round. Both rifles are reliable but with a slight edge to the M-16 in accuracy. The original AK-47 was about a pound and a half heavier than the M-16 but newer productions of the AK-74 the weight is now about equal. AK-74 still used stamped receivers of steel so they weigh about 6.8 pounds with a magazine that weighs about another pound so the AK-74 is still heavier than the M-16. The AK-47 is about 2 pounds heavier than the M-16. Another advantage the AK-47 has over the M16 is cost. For the cost of raw materials, forging, and machining of a M-16 you could manufacture two AK-47's. With the new chrome lined barrel of the AK-74 the Russians have closed the accuracy gap (Though to my way of thinking it wasn't that big of a disadvantage in the first place.) While the M-16 could hit the eye of a gnat at 500 meters most riflemen would be hard pressed to hit a kneeling man at 300 meters.

Now we get down to the nitty gritty. RELIABILITY. From a design perspective the AK-47 is more reliable than the M16 when you consider the rifle alone. The AK-47 as fewer parts that are larger and easier to assemble and disassemble and clean. I would also add the gas system of the M-16 is a weak area when it comes to reliability. With hot gases being dumped into the receiver and different types of metal you get different expansion rates so clearances change drastically. This can allow for carbon build up when the weapon is fired in a heavy engagement but then will malfunction when the weapon cools down. Also the gas impinging system where you have the gas piston in the bolt carrier is a lot more susceptible to foreign object failure (water, sand, dust, mud, etc.) than the gas piston system of the AK-47.

Where the reliability of the AK-47/74 falls apart is in the magazines. the long curved magazine of the AK is a lot more suseptable to failure than the magazine of the M-16. The follower of the AK mag must travel in a arc and will have problems maintaining its proper geometry during its movement. The AK has a lot more failure to feed errors than the M-16. Also along with the magazine I would like to point out that the Russians still use steel cased ammo which is not a reliable as brass ammo. Steel ammo even if lacquered will corrode faster than brass ammo and if the round has been chambered and then removed it will not have it original specifications. Steel cased small arms ammo has a lot more problems than brass ammo.

Now if we consider Ammo alone Russian ammo has always had consistency problems. This is probably why the AK family has had accuracy problems. Russian military ammo is really bad.

So to sum it up. The AK is heavier, simpler, easier to maintain, and mechanically more reliable than the M-16. When you add the banana magazine and steel cased ammo into the equation the reliably of the AK falls off to were the whole weapon system is some what more unreliable than the M-16. This is my opinion.

With modern tactics, accuracy isn't required at a distance. After all, the purpose is to close, not kill at a distance.
